sn55.1:1.3: The legendary wheel-turning monarch, who ruled without violence from sea to sea, is depicted in detail in DN 17 and DN 26. | The four continents (dīpa) are largely mythical, but attempting real world correlations: the Black Plum Tree Land (jambudīpa, India), West of Godāvarī (aparagoyāna, western Asia and Africa; see AN 3.80:4.2 and note), North of Kuru (uttarakuru, central and northern Asia), and East of Videha (pubbavidehāna, eastern Asia). Notably there is no continent to the south of India, suggesting there is at least some geographical reality underlying these places.
sn55.1:2.1: These are the four factors of stream-entry. The devotional passages that follow are regularly recited throughout Theravadin communities, and also form the basis of meditation on the triple gem.
sn55.1:2.2: “Experiential” is avecca, literally “having undergone”. “Experiential confidence” is the faith of a stream-enterer, who has seen for themselves.
sn55.1:2.3: Bhagavā (“blessed one”, “lord”) is the standard honorific for the Buddha in Pali; normally I translate it as “the Buddha”. The literal meaning is “one who has good fortune”, in which sense it stems from Vedic times (Rig Veda 7.41.5). In Pali it is used only for the Buddha, but elsewhere was a general honorific used, for example, by King Janaka to address Yajñavalkya (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14), among respected peers (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.7), to a teacher (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.3), or by Manu to his daughter (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1.9). | Buddha (“awakened one”) is used in Pali especially of Siddhattha Gotama himself, but occasionally as a general term for those who are enlightened. The idea of “awakening” is found throughout the Vedic texts, often associated with the Dawn (RV 1.113.4). | Arahant (“perfected one”, literally “worthy”) is used for the Buddha and others who have realized full awakening. Originally an epithet of the “worthy gods” deserving of praise and sacrifice (eg. RV 1.94.1, 1.127.06, 1.134.6, 5.7.2, 5.52.5, 5.86.5; ŚB 3.4.1.3). | Vijjācaraṇasampanna (“accomplished in knowledge and conduct”) is explained in detail at DN 3. | For sugata (“holy”) see note on SN 38.3:1.4. | Lokavidū may be explained as singular—knowing the cosmos inside a person (SN 2.26)—or plural—knowing the worlds, sometimes numbered three (Tha Ap 535:26.2; cf. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16). | The Buddha’s training is often compared to taming a fine horse or elephant (eg. MN 65:33.1, MN 107:3.2). | The Buddha’s role as teacher of gods is emphasized in SN 1, SN 2, SN 6, and many places throughout the canon.
sn55.1:2.5: Sandiṭṭhika and akālika (“apparent in the present life, immediately effective”) are synonyms, as are anantara and diṭṭheva dhamme, all of which mean “in the present life, without delay or interim”, in contrast with samparāyika (“pertaining to lives to come”; see eg. MN 13:8.5). | Ehipassika (“inviting inspection”) is literally “come-and-see-ish”. | For “relevant”, see note on SN 55.7:3.1. | “Sensible people” is viññū, “knowing ones”. | All these epithets seem primarily Buddhist.
sn55.1:2.7: The suttas distinguish between two senses of Saṅgha. The “mendicant Saṅgha” (bhikkhusaṅgha) is the conventional community of monks and nuns. The “Saṅgha of disciples” (sāvakasaṅgha) is classified as fourfold according to the stages of awakening: stream-entry, once-return, non-return, and perfection. Each of these stages is further subdivided into those of the path who are practicing for realization and those of the fruit who have realized. These are referred to as “noble disciples”, four of the path and four of the fruit, making eight individuals in total. Saṅgha is not used in the sense of “spiritual community”. | “Worthy of hospitality” is literally “to be treated as a guest” (pāhuṇa, see SN 4.18:1.2). | “Religious donation” is dakkhiṇa, the fee paid to Vedic priests for their services; for details see MN 142:5.1. | Añjali is the gesture of raising one’s cupped palms, originally for receiving water or ghee as a ritual gesture (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.4.5.1, 1.9.3.6, 5.3.4.21, 9.4.2.4, 13.8.4.5). | The idea of the “field of merit” is that donations to the Saṅgha yield abundant fruit (see SN 1.33, MN 56, AN 8.59, AN 3.57, AN 8.12, MN 142, etc.). In Sanskrit, puṇyakṣetra is used for a holy place, especially a ford (tīrtha) such as Gayā (Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.82.7) or the Ganges (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 3.40.58).
sn55.1:2.8: This entails keeping the five precepts at a minimum.
